start.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
start.text: {greeting} Mind the desk, the ink is wet and the page is older than the fort.

choices.text: They said you wanted anyone with legs.
I have your bell. There was a page in it.
Who strikes a name out of the Roll?
About Ryn Larkbourne. I have decided.
What is the Roll, exactly?
The Wardens take people on, I hear.
Wren wants the Harewell doorstep out of your box.
Who kept the rolls before the Rest did?
I have the Barrow Reeve's roll. A hundred and forty names.
Who reads at the turn of the season?
Say the privilege again. Slowly.
My hand is on the stone. Hear the name.
About the four hundred years of letters.
Nothing. Keep warm, Roll-Keeper.

the_doorstep.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_doorstep.text: She does. She sent a note about it and the note is longer than the entry the doorstep belongs to. — Shelf under the window, box with the lid that does not fit. Take it. And bring it back, or tell me where it is and who has it, in those words, because the day this room starts holding things that are somewhere else is the day it stops being a Roll room and starts being a cupboard.

barrow_keepers_offer.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
barrow_keepers_offer.text: Barrow-keepers. Reeves. — Before there was a Rest, there was a Reeve to every burying ground, and each of them kept a roll of the people under it, and read it aloud at the turn of the season with the tools written in beside the names. Then somebody at this fort decided that a roll of places was the serious work and a roll of the dead was sentiment, and we split, four hundred years ago, in writing, unpleasantly. — Hollin Barrow never got the letter. There is something down there with a hammer that is still doing the reading, and it is on the forty-first name, and it has been on the forty-first name since before my predecessor's predecessor.

choices.text: You want me to go down and stop it.
You want the roll.
Another time.

barrow_keepers_stop.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
barrow_keepers_stop.text: I want the reading to be done by somebody who can stop. — That is not the same as stopping it, and I am aware I have said a soft thing in a hard voice. He cannot finish. He gets to the end and starts again, and he has been doing it in the cold in the dark for four hundred years, and if you want the Wardens' position on that in one sentence it is this: the office is the reading, not the reader, and an office nobody can be relieved of is not an office, it is a sentence.

choices.text: Then I'll go down and relieve him.
Let me think about it.

barrow_keepers_roll.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
barrow_keepers_roll.text: I want the roll, yes, and I want you to have read it before you hand it over, because I am going to ask you a question afterwards and I will not have it answered by somebody who thinks a hundred and forty is a number. — Take the Standing Orders. They are mostly about lamps. The ninth page is the Keeper's Bond, which is ours, and which is said over whoever goes in first, and which I am not able to say over you because I have never been in first in my life.

choices.text: Then I'll go in first and read it myself.
Let me think about it.

barrow_keepers_accept.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
barrow_keepers_accept.text: Take a lamp that will not go out in a draught, and read the orders before the gate and not on the way down. The bell in the cist is hung, not fallen — somebody put it up there on purpose and it is the only warm thing in that ground, and I have wondered for eleven years which of them thought of it.

the_barrow_names.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_barrow_names.text: A hundred and forty. — Forty minutes. On top of an hour and forty, four times a year, out of that window, to a yard with eleven people and a dog in it. The arithmetic is not the objection and I have now done the arithmetic twice in front of you, so let me be honest about what the objection is: a Roll that takes all afternoon stops being read properly. People start skipping. I have watched a Warden skip and I have never told anybody until this minute. — So. Your hand is on the pen and mine is going to sign under whatever it writes.

choices.text: All hundred and forty. A longer reading is what a reading is.
One line. Hollin Barrow, a hundred and forty, held in the cist.
Leave them out. The Roll keeps places, and a barrow is not a place.
Give me the night to think.

barrow_names_written.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
barrow_names_written.text: Then that is what the Roll says, and my name goes under yours, and in fifty years somebody will read it out loud and mean it. — The Barrow Roll goes on the shelf under the window, next to a chalk doorstep in a box. I have a shelf of things that are the ends of arguments now. Come back at the turn of the season. Somebody has to read.

the_reading_offer.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_reading_offer.text: I do. I have read it every season for nineteen years and I am going to hand it sideways to you this time, which is how this fort promotes anybody and why nobody here has ever had a ceremony. — Five hundred names. An hour and forty. The deep lines first and slowly. Your voice will go at about the fortieth and you will keep going, and that is the entire examination.

choices.text: Give me the book.
Not this season.

the_reading_accept.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_reading_accept.text: Out of the window. Not at the yard; out of the window, at the valley. The yard is not the audience and never was. — Dole will be at the back. He always is, and he never comes in, and he has never once said why, and if he says something to you afterwards you should listen to it, because he has said four things to me in twenty-one years and all four were right.

the_privilege.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_privilege.text: Slowly, then. A Roll-Warden may set a name on a Hearthstone. Hand flat on the stone, say the name aloud, and the stone has it the way it has yours. — Nine times in four hundred years. Twice it was done wrong and I will not be drawn on how, and you may take it from my not being drawn that it was not wrong in a way that hurt the stone. — The one I mean is Ansel's, out on the down between here and Tamwick: a hawthorn grown up through a stone chair with the stone in its lap. It is the only thing left standing on that stretch that anybody walks to on purpose, and I want you to think about why the privilege exists and where I have just sent you with it, and I am not going to say the rest of that sentence.

the_name_on_the_stone.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_name_on_the_stone.text: I am at the field gate and I can hear you perfectly, which I would like you to know I regret. — Say it flat and say it once. A stone is not a yard full of people; it does not need to be convinced. And whatever you say, I will enter in the Roll that it was said, with the date, because the nine times this has been done are the only nine times anybody has written anything down about it.

choices.text: Harewell. Eleven households and a well with a hare on the lip.
My own. I came up out of the quiet with no rope on me.
Ryn Larkbourne. In ink upstairs, and now in stone.
Nothing. A name in one stone is a name in one place.
Give me a moment down here.

the_name_said.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_name_said.text: Then that is nine and one. — Come up. The seal is on my desk and has been since the reading, and I am not going to make a speech about it, because there is nobody above you to make one and I have checked.

the_letter.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_letter.text: Four hundred years of them, in the second press, tied with tape. Ours are shorter than theirs and worse. — The last one from a Reeve is 1041, in a hand I would have said was four hundred years old, and it asks the Rest to send somebody to read at the turn of the season because the writer is finding the forty-first name difficult. It is filed under correspondence, unsolicited. By me. In 1041. I remember doing it and I remember what I thought, and what I thought was that somebody at Hollin was having a joke.

offer.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
offer.text: I did. A tower of ours fell on its side about nine years ago, down the dry valley, and everyone stopped saying its name, and then everyone stopped saying its garrison's names, and now there is a hole in my Roll the shape of eleven people. The hand-bell is still in the ruin. There is a page rolled inside it. I want them both, and I want them in that order, because the page will be ruined if it gets wet and the bell will not.

choices.text: Bandits in it, I take it.
I will bring them back.
Find somebody else.

bandits.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
bandits.text: The Larkbourne Boys, yes. They sleep in the stair, which lies sideways now like a corridor, and they use my bell for a cup. I am not asking you to kill anybody. I am asking you to come back with a bell. What happens between those two sentences is between you and them.

choices.text: I will bring them back.
Not for nothing, I hope.
Find somebody else.

pay.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
pay.text: A hundred and forty marks, a badge you will pretend not to be pleased about, and your name read out at the next season's reading in front of everybody. Two of those three are worth more than they sound.

choices.text: Done.
I will think about it.

accepted.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
accepted.text: West, down the dry valley, and look for a stair going the wrong way. Take a lantern. Come back before you are somebody I have to write down as gone.

returned.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
returned.text: That is it. That is the bell. And the — ah. Ah. Look at that. Somebody has taken a pen to a name and leaned on it. Through the sheet, and into the sheet beneath, which also carries that name, which means whoever did it knew exactly how the Roll is bound and went on anyway.

who_strikes.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
who_strikes.text: A Warden's hand. Only a Warden's. Three of us have had that pen this year and I am one, and I did not, and I would like you to believe that without me having to say it twice. Ask Dole. He drinks at Merrowby on the evenings he is not at the gate, and he has held opinions about this Roll since before you could read.

choices.text: You suspect him.
I will ask him.

suspect.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
suspect.text: I suspect everyone and I accuse nobody; that is the whole of my character and it has cost me friends. Dole is a good Warden. Good Wardens are exactly the people who do a thing like this, because they have decided it will help.

the_pen.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
the_pen.text: The Roll is open. The pen is by the lamp. I am going to see about the fire, which does not need seeing about. Whatever you write, write it clearly: the hand matters as much as the name, and in fifty years somebody will read it out loud and mean it.

choices.text: Put Ryn Larkbourne back on the Roll.
Strike it properly, and be done.
Give me the night to think.

restored.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
restored.text: There. Written, and witnessed, and read aloud badly by me. Whatever Ryn Larkbourne does with a name back is Ryn Larkbourne's to do. That is not comfort. It is just how it works.

struck.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
struck.text: Then it is struck, and I will sign under it so that the hand is mine as well as yours, because I will not let you carry that alone. It is the safer thing. I do not think it is the right one, and I have been wrong about which is which before.

about_the_roll.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
about_the_roll.text: Every settlement in the basin, written down, with who spoke for it and the season it was read. We read it aloud at the Rest four times a year, all of it, out of the window, badly. People laugh at us. Then a hamlet goes quiet on the fringe and everyone comes here to find out what it was called, and nobody laughs that week.

choices.text: Does it work?
Back to it.

does_it_work.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
does_it_work.text: Three hamlets have gone quiet since I took the pen. I can still say all three names. My predecessor could say four, and two of those have people living in them again. Make of that what you like; the Sayers certainly do.

join_talk.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
join_talk.text: We do. It is not a dashing life. You will hold a lantern, you will walk a road at night, and once a season you will stand in a cold yard while somebody reads out five hundred names and gets some of them wrong.

choices.text: Put me down for it.
I will think about it.

joined.speaker: core:npc/wardens_hesk
joined.text: Then you are a Lantern-bearer, and your name is on the inside cover where we keep our own. Try not to make me move it to the other list.

choices.text: You struck a name out of the Roll.
You struck a name out of the Roll.
Hesk speaks well of you, mostly.
You were at the back of the yard. Say it, then.
Nothing. Enjoy your evening.

admits.speaker: core:npc/wardens_dole
admits.text: I did. Sit down, you are making the room look at us. Yes, I struck Ryn Larkbourne, and I pressed hard, and I would do it again on a worse evening than this one. You have read what the Roll is for. Now think about what it does. A name holds a thing together. Put a bandit's name in a book that four hundred people hear read out and you have not recorded a bandit, you have built one a banner.

choices.text: So you took a person apart to stop a band forming.
That was not your pen to use that way.
You have done this before.

took_apart.speaker: core:npc/wardens_dole
took_apart.text: I took a banner down. Whether there was a person behind it is a thing the Roll does not measure and neither do I, standing on the Larkbourne road at two in the morning with a carter bleeding into my coat. Go and look at Ryn, if you like. Gosling Pit, under the Hound. Look properly, and then tell me I am the one doing the damage.

not_your_pen.speaker: core:npc/wardens_dole
not_your_pen.text: No. It was Hesk's, and Hesk would have said no with his whole chest and then gone back to his ink. Tell him. He will write my name in a smaller column and we will both keep doing this until one of us is quiet. Ryn is at Gosling Pit. See it yourself before you decide anything with a pen.

before.speaker: core:npc/wardens_dole
before.text: ...Twice. The other one deserved it more and it worked less. You are quick. Do not be quick at Hesk, he takes it badly. Ryn is at Gosling Pit. Go and see what a struck name looks like when it is still walking about.

the_yard.speaker: core:npc/wardens_dole
the_yard.text: Your voice went at Larkstead and you carried on. Good. — I stand at the back because I can hear which names the reader hurries. Hesk hurries Gosford, every season, nineteen years, and does not know he does it, and I have never told him because he would stop reading it altogether rather than read it badly. You hurried nothing. You hurried nothing and you were slower on Harewell than on the others, which is the first time anybody has been, and I noticed, and now you know that somebody in that yard is counting as well as listening.

about_hesk.speaker: core:npc/wardens_dole
about_hesk.text: He is the best of us and he has never once stood on a road at night. Both of those are true and he knows both of them, which is why I drink here and he reads there.

start.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
start.text: Stop there. Hands where the fire can see them.

not_now.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
not_now.text: Wrong pit, wrong evening. Go on.

hub.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
hub.text: Well? You are not a carter and you are not the Watch, so you are something newer and worse.

choices.text: A Warden struck your name out of the Roll.
What is happening to you?
The mill wheel. Pennywort wants it back.
Nothing yet.

the_striking.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
the_striking.text: I know. I have known since the spring, because that is when the boys started calling me you. Not Ryn. You. And when I say the name to them they agree with it, politely, the way you agree with a drunk about the weather. Somebody put a pen through me and I have been thinning out ever since, and the worst of it is that it is working. Nobody is riding out to join me. There is no band. There is a pit, a wheel, and four lads who cannot hold my name in their heads past a rainy afternoon.

choices.text: You put a thumb in a carter's ribs for a mill wheel.
What do you want written?

the_carter.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
the_carter.text: Tam did that, and Tam is dead of it, and I have not said that out loud to anyone because there is nobody left who can hold on to a sentence about me for long enough to hear the end of it. I am not asking to be forgiven. I am asking to be findable. Strike me properly if you must, but somebody ought to be able to say what it was they struck.

what_you_want.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
what_you_want.text: My name back, and then the Watch can come and take it off me honestly, in front of people, with my name being said the whole time. That is the difference and I know how thin it sounds. A person who is hanged is remembered. A person who is rubbed out is not even that.

choices.text: I will put you back on the Roll.
I have not decided.
You are safer rubbed out, and so is everyone else.

promised.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
promised.text: Then say it in the yard where they can hear it, not in a pit where only I can. And tell Dole it was a good idea. It very nearly worked.

undecided.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
undecided.text: Decide soon. I have started forgetting which of my brothers is the tall one.

refused.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
refused.text: Aye. Probably. Go on then, and mind the loose chalk on the way up, because it would be a poor joke if the pit got you and nobody could say who it got.

fading.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
fading.text: I go quiet. Bit by bit, the way the hamlets do. It is not dying; it is being mislaid. Ask your Roll-Keeper what he thinks that means about the rest of us, and watch his face do the thing where it stops.

wheel.speaker: core:npc/wardens_ryn
wheel.text: It is a table now. Take it if you can lift it, and tell Pennywort the flour was better when the wheel was stopped, which is a joke, and which he will not find funny, which is also the joke.
